1:
The psalm's title divides the voices before its first line does. Calvin reports that the Jewish expositors are not of one mind, some deriving the word so that the psalm is fit to be written in letters of gold, others so that it is fit to be engraven on a durable pillar and preserved in everlasting remembrance. Clarke adds the Chaldee, which makes it a straight sculpture of David, and the sense of pure or stamped gold, by which it becomes a golden psalm; but he has already expressed his doubts about the meanings given to such titles and does not settle this one. Henry takes the golden sense and supplies a reason the others do not: the psalm is more to be valued than much fine gold because it speaks so plainly of Christ and his resurrection, who is the true treasure hidden in the field of the Old Testament.

Who speaks in the psalm is the larger question, and the answers run the whole range. Clarke is the most absolute: from the most serious consideration of the whole he is convinced that every verse of it belongs to Jesus Christ and none other, and he takes the opening prayer for the words of the man Christ Jesus entering on his atoning work in the garden. Augustine had read it the same way, that our King speaks here in the character of the human nature he assumed. Gill agrees that prayer is proper to Christ as man, and applies the petition to the preserving of that life, from the rage of Herod to the enemies who could not take it before his time. Henry reads David first and Christ by application, noting at each turn that the verse is applicable to him who prayed to be saved from his hour. Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin keep to David throughout, the one finding a writer in danger of death whose cry for help is immediately swallowed up by blessed consciousness and bright hope, the other simply that David commends himself to God's protection and then meditates on the benefits he has received.

Clarke's reading of the first verse turns on the divine name. The verb he renders as a plea to keep and sustain this feeble humanity under the load it was about to bear; and he observes that the word used for God here is the one signifying the strong God, remarkably suited to the frailty of a nature just entering on its vicarious sufferings, the Messiah varying the appellations of the Divine Being with a propriety no translation can express. Ellicott's note goes the other way: the verb is in the preterite, and the clause should read that the speaker has found refuge in God.

The second verse brings the real collision. Henry, Clarke, Wesley and Spurgeon all build on the received sense, that whatever good we do extends not to God, so that we cannot pretend to merit anything by it. Henry puts it that God has no need of our services and is happy without us, so that we are indebted to him and not he to us. Spurgeon presses it furthest, that God would have been inconceivably glorious had the race perished and no atonement been offered. Gill defends even the supplied words of the address, which are not in the original but are confirmed to him by the Targum and by three Jewish commentators. Ellicott undercuts the whole structure. The text of the passage, he holds, is exceedingly corrupt, the ancient versions agree against the received reading, the words about the soul are a mere gloss, the following verse is unintelligible as it stands, and the fine thought that merit lives from man to man and not from man to God cannot have been the thought of the original, since the good in question means happiness and not conduct.
3:
The saints to whom the speaker's goodness does extend are identified in four ways. Gill makes them those set apart by the Father in election, whose sins are expiated by the blood of Christ and who are sanctified by the Spirit in the effectual calling, and explains the phrase about the earth as pointing to the place of their abode, scattered up and down in it, perhaps distinguishing them from the angels, who are also called saints. Henry takes it as a standing requirement, that saints on earth we must all be or we shall never be saints in heaven, and holds the paradox that these are the excellent ones, made so by the grace given them, and yet some so poor in this world that they needed David's goodness extended to them; and he adds that it is not enough to delight in them, since our goodness must reach them in the kindness they need. Augustine reads the earth in the other direction, of the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem whose conversation is fixed by the anchor of hope in that country, rightly called God's earth, although they are as yet conversant in the flesh here. Clarke suggests the first planters of Christianity, the apostles consecrated to preaching among the Gentiles, and allows that the angels may be intended, since they desire to look into these things.

Two voices will not take the verse as the others do. Wesley grants the sense but refuses the reference, observing that it agrees more properly with David than with Christ, whose goodness was principally designed for sinners and imparted to them. Ellicott will not take the verse as it stands at all, calling it quite unintelligible and requiring emendation, and proposes dropping the conjunction and allowing one of those changes of person agreeable to Hebrew, so that the saints in the earth are themselves the excellent in whom is all the speaker's delight.

On the multiplied sorrows of those who hasten after another god the readings diverge again. Henry gives the plainest sense and the sharpest epigram: idolaters are mad upon their idols and pursue them as though afraid they would escape, and those who multiply gods multiply griefs to themselves, since whoever thinks one God too little will find two too many and yet hundreds not enough. Clarke notes that the Hebrew has no word for God in the clause, so that Messiah might be substituted, and applies the whole to those who would not have the true Christ and are still seeking another; he also reports that the Greek and Latin versions turn it quite differently, making the afflictions those of persecuted saints who ran the more swiftly the more they suffered. Ellicott finds the ancient versions varying greatly here too, renders it that they shall multiply their sorrows who change to another god, and observes that the verb can mean to buy a wife, so that the prophets' figure of idolatry as adultery was probably in the psalmist's mind, though he does not work it out. The libations the speaker refuses are read as the rites of Moloch and Chemosh by Ellicott, and Clarke objects to the English phrase, since the libation was poured on the blood of a sacrifice already made rather than being a drink-offering of blood. Henry supplies the contrast that makes the refusal pointed: at God's altar the drinking of blood was strictly forbidden and the drink-offerings were of wine, but the devil prescribed the blood of the sacrifices to his worshippers in order to teach them cruelty. On refusing even to name those gods, Ellicott remarks that to the Hebrews a god's very name included a claim about his power, which is why one such name was avoided and a word meaning a shameful thing put in its place, even inside proper names.
5:
Both the portion and the cup are read against the Levitical background. Gill has Christ speak here as a priest, in allusion to the priests who had no inheritance in Canaan with their brethren but had the Lord for their part, and takes the verse for his delight in serving, since it was his meat and drink to do that will. Ellicott finds the same allusion in the law that made God himself the priestly portion, and asks us to imagine the poet exiled from his actual inheritance, consoling himself, and more than consoling himself, with the thought that this better part could not be taken from him; he quotes a saying gathered by Perowne, that a man who possesses the possessor of all cannot want for possessions, and sets beside it the apostle's word that all things are yours because you are Christ's. Clarke, hearing the Messiah throughout, makes the lot given him the redemption of mankind and the cup a cup of suffering drunk for their sake, through which he imparts to them the cup of consolation. Wesley keeps to the plainer image of a feast, where each guest had his portion of meat and his wine allotted to him.

The clause about maintaining the lot draws a grammatical note and a doctrinal one. Ellicott reports that the Hebrew word is peculiar and causes difficulties, though the sense is clear enough: God does not merely cast a man's lot, which he does even for unbelievers, but holds it fast in his hand; and he thinks a conjectural emendation giving the sense that God is himself ever the speaker's lot very plausible. Keil and Delitzsch work from the practice behind the figure, where the measuring cords are cast and fall just so far as a man's property is assigned to him, and conclude that the lines have fallen to this man in a charming district, namely the fellowship of God, which has become his paradisaic possession. Henry puts the same confidence in the first person, that he who has promised to be ours will never leave us to forfeit the happiness nor leave it in our enemies' power to rob us of it, since nothing shall pluck us out of his hands.

Whether the pleasant places are places at all is disputed. Gill argues for persons rather than places, the lines marking out the chosen ones given to Christ as his portion, pleasant to him as he saw them in his Father's purposes and as they will be when adorned for him in the New Jerusalem; he notes that the word for places is a supplement made by two Jewish commentators. Clarke reads it the same way and makes the heritage an inheritance of immortal spirits, an innumerable multitude who shall dwell with him for ever. Ellicott keeps to the land and explains that the cords are said to fall because the measured portions were then distributed by lot. Spurgeon turns the verse on the obedience that led there, finding it strange but credible that the man most thoroughly acquainted with grief should also have known more joy in service than any other, since the joy set before him sent some of its splendour down the rugged places where he endured the cross; and he adds that discontented spirits are as unlike Jesus as the croaking raven is unlike the cooing dove, martyrs having been happy in dungeons. Henry draws the rule that fits every reading of it: gracious persons, though they still covet more of God, never covet more than God, and those whose lot is cast in a land of light have reason to say the lines have fallen pleasantly, much more those who have not only the means but the end, not only Immanuel's land but Immanuel's love.
7:
The counsel the speaker blesses God for is read both of the gift and of the organ receiving it. Clarke takes it that Jesus as man received all his knowledge and wisdom from God, and then dwells on the word rendered reins, the kidneys, which from their retired situation in the body and their being hidden in fat were used for the most secret workings of the heart, and which with their fat were burnt in sacrifice to signify that the soul's most secret purposes are to be devoted to God; the night seasons he takes for the time of the passion. Ellicott prefers to render the verb as warning rather than instructing, since conscience echoes the voice of God and the Hebrew root carries the sense of binding, so that once heard the divine monition becomes a law to a good man and his own heart warns him of the least deviation. Henry says the same by another road: when a man is silent and retired from the world, his conscience not only reflects with comfort on the choice he has made but admonishes him about the duties arising out of it, and those who have God for their portion must give their consciences leave to deal so plainly with them. Wesley keeps the picture domestic, that even when others are asleep the mind is working upon God and improving the silence for holy meditation.

At the next verse Wesley marks a turn, and in doing so takes a position the chapter's other Christological reader denies. Hitherto, he says, David seems to have spoken with respect to himself, but now he is transported by the spirit of prophecy and carried above himself, to speak as a type of Christ, in whom this and the following verses were truly accomplished. Clarke recognises no such transition, having held from the first that every verse belongs to Christ and none other, noting only that this verse and all to the end are applied by the apostle to Christ's death and resurrection. Henry records the same apostolic use and adds that, Christ being the head of the body, these verses may be applied to all Christians, so that it is our duty to set the Lord always before us. Gill guards the object of the setting, which is not the fear of God only, nor the book of the law as one Jewish commentator interprets it, but the Lord himself.

On the assurance that follows, each voice supplies a different ground. Ellicott finds the image a military one, the shield of the right-hand comrade protecting the man beside him. Clarke reads it as constant presence, approbation and support, all of it spoken by Christ as man, so that nothing can swerve him from his purpose. Gill makes it an eye to the Father's glory as the end of every action, to his orders as the rule of them, and to his faithfulness for support in the most distressed circumstances. Spurgeon adds the one thing the others omit, that the fear of death did once cast its dark shadow over the Redeemer's soul and that an angel came to strengthen him; after which hope shone full upon him, and he stayed not his hand until he could say that it was finished.

Keil and Delitzsch read the closing strophe as a whole and find in it no need to fear death at all, the nearness of God making the heart joyful and the joy breaking out into rejoicing. They notice further that the three terms used here of the man, his heart, his glory and his flesh, answer to the spirit, soul and body of the apostle's prayer that his readers be preserved blameless, so that what he desires for them David expresses as a confident expectation; no passage of Scripture, they say, so closely resembles this one.
9:
The three things said to rejoice are the heart, the glory and the flesh, and what the middle term means is unsettled. Clarke reports that the Hebrews called the tongue a man's glory, since it was given to glorify God, though he allows that soul bids as fair to be the meaning; Wesley keeps the tongue, a man's privilege above all other creatures. Ellicott conjectures a different vowelling that would give the liver, or, as with the reins earlier, the heart, and notes that the Greek translators paraphrased it as the tongue. Ellicott parts company with the others on the hope: the familiar rendering follows the Latin and the Greek has the flesh tabernacle in hope, but the true rendering, he says, is that it shall rest in security.

The verse about Sheol and corruption is where the chapter's two readings become incompatible. Clarke states his flatly: there is no sense in which these and the following words can be spoken of David, and holds that Jesus even on the cross saw his rest in the grave would be long enough to prove his death real but too short to produce corruption. Gill works carefully to the same end, ruling out the place of the damned, where Christ never went, and concluding that it seems best of all to read the word of the grave, so that what was not left there was his body. Ellicott dismantles the argument at its hinge. The word rendered corruption he takes for a pit, from a root meaning to sink in, so that to be left to Sheol and to see the pit are simply synonyms for dying, and the clear meaning of the passage is that God will not abandon his beloved to death. He adds the warning that we must not see a conscious reference to immortality here, while granting what makes his position more than negative: in this psalm we discern the first faint scintillation of the light of immortality, the veil over the individual's future being stirred, if not lifted, by the morning breath of a larger faith, and it is this that justifies the use made of the passage in the New Testament.

On one textual question the two converge. The received Hebrew has thy holy ones in the plural, and both notice it. Clarke observes that none of the versions translate it so, that the singular stands in several ancient editions and in a great many collated manuscripts, and that the apostle quotes it in the singular twice, so that either the present reading is a corruption or the plural is emphatic. Ellicott adds that the received text itself carries a marginal note calling the sign of the plural superfluous, and finds the weight of manuscript authority, of the ancient versions and of the New Testament quotations all on the side of the singular.

The last verse is read by everyone as the end the psalm has been moving toward. Gill takes the path of life for the resurrection, shown to Christ not by instruction but by his being raised, he being the first to tread it and so the firstfruits of them that slept. Clarke notes that the word for life is plural, proper enough since the resurrection implies the life of body and rational soul together; and he reads the pleasures as an eternal progression, so that however far one extends the thought of duration there is still more. Wesley sets the contrast plainly: our pleasures here are momentary, while at God's right hand are the pleasures of immortal souls enjoying an eternal God. Ellicott complains only that the supplied words of the English spoil a triplet, and reads it as one more image of the psalm's dominating thought, the happiness of being with God, a settled satisfaction touched, ever so faintly, by a ray of a larger hope beginning to triumph over death.
